title: How Google Maps knows there’s traffic
musicPrompt: Calm, curious lo-fi electronic bed for a two-minute explainer, about 90 BPM, soft plucked synth arpeggio, warm sub bass, light clock-like hi-hats, a lift around 60 seconds when the roads turn into dots and lines, steady build through the route-finding section, and a gentle resolve in the last 12 seconds, instrumental, no vocals.

scenes.text: How does Google Maps know about a traffic jam before you even reach it?
Welcome to How It Scales, by Curiously.
In 2020, an artist in Berlin pulled ninety-nine second-hand phones through the streets in a handcart. On Google Maps, those streets turned red.
That's the first clue. Google pools location data from lots of people's phones. When many of them crawl along one road, Google can tell it's slow.
Drivers' incident reports add closures and roadworks, and local governments add speed limits and tolls.
But a jam right now isn't enough. You need the traffic ten, twenty, even fifty minutes into your drive.
So Google also remembers how each road usually flows. One California freeway moves at sixty-five miles an hour early in the morning, but fifteen to twenty in the late afternoon.
When lockdowns emptied the roads in 2020, Google started trusting the last two to four weeks of patterns more than older ones.
To forecast, Google teamed up with DeepMind, an Alphabet AI lab. They split roads into supersegments: runs of connected road that share a lot of traffic.
Then comes a graph neural network. Picture every stretch of road as a dot, with lines joining stretches that connect.
Neighbouring dots pass messages to each other, so the model learns how a jam on a side street spills onto a bigger road.
The model predicts a travel time for each supersegment. Google uses those to work out your ETA, your estimated time of arrival, for every possible route.
scenes.say: The model predicts a travel time for each supersegment. Google uses those to work out your E.T.A., your estimated time of arrival, for every possible route.

scenes.text: It ranks the routes by ETA And if it predicts traffic building ahead, it finds you a lower-traffic way around.
scenes.say: It ranks the routes by E.T.A. And if it predicts traffic building ahead, it finds you a lower-traffic way around.

scenes.text: In 2020, Google said its arrival times were accurate for over ninety-seven percent of trips.
So before you get there, phones already stuck in the jam have helped tell Google. Even phones in a handcart.
